children.value: The other NEXRAD notebooks in this cookbook read
data: the full radar volume, every sweep and every moment, about 18 MB per volume. The same radars also publish

products, generated at each site by the Radar Product Generator. A Level III file holds a single product (one tilt of one moment, or a derived quantity such as one-hour rainfall or hydrometeor class), it is 50 to 300 times smaller than the volume it came from, and it is the form in which the National Weather Service itself distributes and displays NEXRAD data. The Unidata-managed
bucket on AWS Open Data carries these products for every WSR-88D within minutes of each scan, with an archive reaching back to 30 March 2020 (the super-resolution
products joined the feed in February and March 2022).
This notebook works through the morning of
, when a squall line crossed southeast Texas and produced two brief tornadoes near Houston, using the KHGX (Houston/Galveston) radar. We will:
Learn the product catalog and how the bucket is organized
List a directory-less bucket efficiently with key prefixes
Read base reflectivity and velocity at the time of a tornado
Compare a Level III reflectivity product with the Level II sweep it came from
Build a rainfall time series at points from the one-hour accumulation product
Map the storm-total accumulation and compare it with rain gauges
Find the newest scan for near-real-time use, including the “no precipitation” case
Looking at NEXRAD Data from Moore, Oklahoma
The Level II workflow this notebook complements

children.value: A WSR-88D completes a volume scan every four to ten minutes. The raw moments from every sweep of that volume (reflectivity, velocity, spectrum width and the three dual-polarization moments) make up
. The Radar Product Generator at the site then turns the volume into

: a few dozen files, each holding one tilt of one moment or one derived quantity, already quality-controlled, quantized, and ready to display. Each product has a three-character mnemonic and a numeric product code. The products you will meet most often, with the code Py-ART uses to identify them:
Base reflectivity, super-resolution, lowest four tilts
Differential reflectivity, correlation coefficient, specific differential phase, hydrometeor classification
One-hour and storm-total accumulation from the legacy single-polarization algorithm
reads every product above into an ordinary
object with a single sweep and a single field. Not every product in the bucket is covered: a few are graphics or tables rather than radial images (
on them, while the enhanced echo tops (
) open but come back without a field.

Level III costs you the vertical structure (one tilt per file) and the ability to re-process the raw moments. In exchange you get files that read in a fraction of a second, derived products that would take real effort to reproduce from Level II (the dual-polarization rainfall estimates in particular), and the exact fields that forecasters look at.
Every object in the bucket sits at the top level. There are no year or site folders; the whole structure is in the key:
is the radar’s four-letter identifier with the leading
for a Terminal Doppler Weather Radar) removed, so KHGX becomes
is the three-character mnemonic from the table above.
The timestamp is the UTC start time of the volume scan the product was generated from, which is also the timestamp in the matching Level II file name.
A flat bucket with hundreds of products per radar every few minutes holds billions of keys, so listing it wholesale (
) never finishes. The bucket is designed to be listed by
: S3 only walks the keys that match, so
returns the ten one-hour accumulation files KHGX produced between 12:00 and 12:59 UTC and nothing else.
We will use the same anonymous S3 filesystem as the Level II notebooks and wrap the listing in a small helper that returns a tidy table.

BUCKET = "unidata-nexrad-level3"
fs = fsspec.filesystem("s3", anon=True)


def key_time(key):
    """UTC datetime encoded in a Level III key, SITE_PROD_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS."""
    parts = key.split("_")
    return datetime(*map(int, parts[2:8]), tzinfo=timezone.utc)


def list_level3(site, product, prefix):
    """Level III files for one site and product whose timestamp starts with ``prefix``.

    ``prefix`` can be as coarse as a day ("2022_03_22") or as fine as a minute
    ("2022_03_22_12_20").  One bounded S3 LIST request either way.
    """
    found = fs.find(BUCKET, prefix=f"{site}_{product}_{prefix}", detail=True)
    rows = []
    for path, info in sorted(found.items()):
        key = path.split("/", 1)[1]
        rows.append({"key": key, "time": key_time(key), "bytes": info["size"]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


list_level3("HGX", "DAA", "2022_03_22_12")
accepts a file-like object, so we open the key with
and hand it over. Nothing is written to disk.

def read_level3(key):
    """Read one Level III product straight from S3 into a Py-ART Radar object."""
    with fs.open(f"{BUCKET}/{key}", "rb") as f:
        return pyart.io.read_nexrad_level3(f)


radar = read_level3("HGX_N0B_2022_03_22_12_01_25")
print(f"fields:        {list(radar.fields)}")
print(f"sweeps:        {radar.nsweeps} at {radar.fixed_angle['data'][0]:.1f} degrees")
print(f"rays x gates:  {radar.nrays} x {radar.ngates}")
print(f"max range:     {radar.range['data'].max() / 1000:.0f} km")
print(f"scan time:     {radar.time['units']}")

children.value: A warm front lifted north across Texas on 21 March 2022. Long-track supercells formed along the dryline that afternoon and produced tornadoes from south-central Texas into the northern counties of the Houston forecast area through the evening. Overnight a squall line organized along the cold front and crossed southeast Texas during the early morning of 22 March. The bowing segment of that line produced two brief tornadoes: an EF1 near Beasley in Fort Bend County at 5:35 AM CDT (10:35 UTC) that injured four people in an RV, and an EF0 at Danbury in Brazoria County at 7:21 AM CDT (12:21 UTC). Rain gauges across the Houston metro recorded one to two and a half inches in the few hours it took the line to pass. The National Weather Service’s
has the full tornado list and the gauge reports we will use later.

children.value: The lowest sweep has the same number of valid gates and the same maximum in both files. The Level III product is the Level II sweep after the Radar Product Generator’s processing: the same 0.5 dB quantization, the same 720 super-resolution radials, eight more range gates because the product’s range axis starts at the antenna rather than at the first Level II gate. Everything else in the volume (the other 20 sweeps, velocity, spectrum width and the dual-polarization moments) is what the 50-fold difference in size and read time buys.

children.value: ) is where Level III earns its keep. The product is the output of the WSR-88D’s quantitative precipitation estimation chain: hydrometeor classification removes non-meteorological echoes, a rate is estimated gate by gate from reflectivity, differential reflectivity and specific differential phase, and the rate is integrated over the trailing hour. Reproducing that from Level II is a project; reading it is one line. Py-ART stores the field as
with units of inches per hour, which over a one-hour window is the same number as inches of accumulation.

Py-ART computes a latitude and longitude for every gate, so “the accumulation at this address” is the value of the nearest gate. The helper below returns zero rather than a masked value where the product reports no precipitation, which is what the question “how much rain fell here?” needs.

def distance_km(radar, lat, lon):
    """Great-circle distance in km from every gate of ``radar`` to a point."""
    gate_lat = np.radians(radar.gate_latitude["data"])
    gate_lon = np.radians(radar.gate_longitude["data"])
    lat, lon = np.radians(lat), np.radians(lon)
    h = (np.sin((gate_lat - lat) / 2) ** 2
         + np.cos(lat) * np.cos(gate_lat) * np.sin((gate_lon - lon) / 2) ** 2)
    return 2 * 6371.0 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(h))


def value_at(radar, lat, lon, field="radar_estimated_rain_rate"):
    """Field value in the gate nearest to (lat, lon); 0.0 where the product is masked."""
    data = radar.fields[field]["data"]
    nearest = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(distance_km(radar, lat, lon)), data.shape)
    value = data[nearest]
    return 0.0 if np.ma.is_masked(value) else float(value)

Conroe, 60 km north of downtown, peaks first at about 11:30 UTC; Bush Intercontinental follows half an hour later, downtown by 12:30, Hobby by 13:00, and Galveston on the coast at 14:00. Each curve rises as rain falls and decays over the following hour as the trailing window slides past it. The two tornado times sit exactly where the line passes the corresponding counties.
Hobby airport and downtown Houston are 15 km apart and their peak one-hour totals differ by a quarter, which is the kind of gradient a single rain gauge cannot see and a 1 km radar product can.

children.value: The comparison is fair in time: the one-hour product stayed empty at all five airports from 15:00 UTC to midnight, so both the storm total and the daily gauge reading cover the same rain. It is not flattering everywhere. The radar matches the gauges at Hobby and Sugar Land but reports half again as much at Bush Intercontinental, Hooks and Conroe, where the line was most intense. Overestimation in the cores of convective lines is a known behavior of radar rainfall estimation (hail and large drops raise reflectivity faster than the rain rate, and the relationships behind the algorithm are tuned for stratiform rain), and it is why operational products such as MRMS and the NWS stage-IV analysis bias-correct radar against gauges before anyone uses the numbers for hydrology. A Level III accumulation is an excellent map of
; treat the magnitudes as a first estimate.
New products land in the bucket within minutes of the scan, which makes the Level III bucket a live feed as well as an archive. Finding the newest file is a prefix problem again. Listing
returns the first thousand keys in lexical order, which are the oldest keys from March 2022; the right move is to list today’s date prefix, and yesterday’s if today is empty.
Two things change when you read live data:
Rain products exist only when there is rain. When the radar detects no precipitation anywhere in its coverage, the
files are a few hundred bytes long and carry a text message instead of a radial image. Py-ART raises
the answer, so the helper below returns
rather than walking back in time to find a product that decodes.
The reflectivity products always decode, whatever the weather, so
is the right product for a “what does the radar see right now” picture.
